blocks.x: Okay, it's going. If you just wanted to get, just sit up so you don't have to worry about getting close to it or anything, just any place in the room.

Tell who it is speaking. This is Maurice Durand speaking. Should I tell him my address? Yes. 2281A Sutter Street, San Francisco. I'm from New Orleans, and I born July the 4th, 1893, St. Menard Parish. Down below the city limits? Yes, below the city limits. And I first started to play music when I was about 10, 12 years old. My uncle was a musician. He used to play with the Terminal Brass Band. Which band is that? Terminal.
Oh, the Terminal.
Terminal Brass Band, yeah. And he gave me my first lesson. And then after that, I was taking lessons from Professor Humphrey.
That was old Jim.
Yeah, Jim Humphrey.
I was going to ask about your family. Did your parents, father and mother play anything?
No, my father never played, or my mother either. Only my uncle, I had two uncles who were musicians.
They had the same name as you, Durand?
No, no. My uncle who had loaned me was Pierre. My family name was Pierre Durand. I mean Pierre. Yeah. See, my name is Durand, see.
What is your middle? Do you have a middle name?
No, no middle name. No middle name. No.
I wondered about, not to worry about your religion and all, I just wondered if you were a Catholic, was it downtown?
Oh yeah, I'm Catholic. I was, yeah, I'm Catholic.
Did you learn on any other instrument first? What was your first instrument that you started on?

Well the first, the only one was the trumpet. It was the only instrument I played, was trumpet. And I played with different bands, you know, like Buddy P.D., Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, and a lot of jazz bands. And I played with Manuel Perez, Tuxedo Brass Band, Armwood Brass Band, and I also played with Fess Mineta. And Al J.
Tell about that, when you used to play with him.

Oh, him and I used to play, he had the accordion, you know. And he'd come down home and pick me up, and him and I would go out on there and play, you know, little parties, you know, to get together, you know, like that.
Also orchestra.

Yeah, we played in the orchestra on the Parisian roof garden, with Emmanuel Perez's band. And then after we left there, why, uh, uh, Emmanuel and I made a brass band up together, the Armwood Brass Band.
Emmanuel Perez.
Yeah, Emmanuel Perez. See?
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, also a lot of places that I played. We, my band was, uh, Durant and Humphrey, you remember Fess?
Yes.
Durant and Humphrey.
Which Humphrey was that?
That was Willie.
Young Willie Humphrey.
Young Willie Humphrey. Yeah, the clarinet. See, his father taught me how to play, you know.
Or was it his grandfather?
No, his grandfather. His grandfather taught him.
Jim Humphrey.
Jim Humphrey. Yeah.
Because his father was Willie too.
Oh, yeah.
Mm-hmm. And mention them in the, in the orchestra, you had your orchestra. The, uh, Durant and Humphrey.
Yeah. Yeah.
Who else is in that band?

Well, in Durant and Humphrey band? Mm-hmm. We had, uh, Bebe Mathis on drum. Willie, uh, Buddy Johnson, trombone, I'm playing trumpet. Willie Humphrey, clarinet. And a fellow by the name of Green playing banjo. And, uh, Jimmy Johnson was playing bass. Mm-hmm. Oh, we had a wonderful band. Pretty good band.

Well, I was going to go way back again, a little bit slower on your life. Do you remember when you were just a little kid, the first music you heard? The first, yeah. The first, yeah. The first, bands or what were they?

Well, I used to follow up, uh, uh, Freddie Kepit all the time, you know. And, uh, Big Al Louie. Louie DeLia is writing there. Yeah. I agree. Very well. Yeah. And I used to go up on the stand and say, uh, Mr. Freddie, would you let me play a little piece? And he'd say, sure. And I couldn't play it but a full piece. I wish I could shimmy like my sister Kate, I forgot the others, you know. And I'd play that and so Louie would say, what are you going to play it now, son? I'd say, play it right over again, same thing over again. So we'd play that over. So Louie got tired playing the same thing over and he'd say, ta-ta-ta-ta. He'd call Freddie and say, come on Freddie and play. And I remember the first piece I played when I could play a trumpet was a six-eight march called Shoulder Strap. You remember that first? Yeah. Shoulder Strap. That was the, my uncle band had that number. You know, a terminal brass band. They had it.
Do you remember who else was in that terminal band? Any other famous musicians?

Well the only one that I can remember is Sonny Hendry. I think he was playing bass at that time. And Norm Monetta, Paul Pierre and Brazier was the leader of the band. He played trumpet. And another fellow played trombone called Louie Rodriguez I think is his name. But that's all I can think about, they played in that band.
That was a brass band that would march in the streets.
Yeah. They were strictly, you know, parade and funeral bands, you know.
Did you follow those bands when you were a kid like all the other bands?
Oh yeah, I used to follow Manuel Perez and Joe Oliver and all those fellas. Freddie Kepard, used to follow all them fellas.
Who was your favorite trumpet player in those days? Did you have a favorite? Yeah, I did.

Did you like better than anybody else? Yeah, I certainly did. My favorite trumpet player was Manuel Perez. I went to him to get some lessons, you know, take lessons from him. Well he had his hand full. You see, he couldn't take me, but he recommended Professor Humphrey. That's how I started taking lessons from him. How long did you take lessons from Humphrey? Oh, I guess I'd take lessons from him about a year. See, then he enticed Willie and I to make a band up together. That's how we come to make the band up.
Remember the method book you used?

Auburn? The Auburn Method. Oh, I went through the Auburn. Through the Auburn Method. And then after that, I got acquainted with Fess Moneta, and I started going over by his house, and he was giving a few ideas too, you know, on the trumpet. And we would play duets together. And that's how I come to be friendly with him.

What was that one job you told me once about Fess when you were playing, that old man Albert Blinney and all of us, at some party they were at? Oh, and he was out there, Saturday night, and caught in the trumpet.

And he was all down at night, he was around his friend and my friend. Way down there. Knock off, he'd come up and say, let's take a little run around this house here. And late around after one o'clock in the morning, and they had a ball there. He was cutting up there, he was in there with old Auburn, playing there. And then, that bass player, I call his name another night, Willie Predonce. Johnny Predonce. Johnny Predonce. Johnny Predonce. Yeah, Johnny Predonce. And we get in there and we start to play.

Do you remember anything about that bass player? Because once when I asked Albert Blinney who was the first one that he ever heard pick on the bass, and slap it and all that, he thought that this, I can't pronounce the name Predonce. Predonce?
Predonce, yeah. Johnny Predonce. I think that's it.
Do you remember anything about him when you were, he must have been pretty young when you first heard him, I guess?
Well, I'll tell you, he played with, uh, Willie and Joe. Joe Nicholas. That's my sister Kate, Jessica A. Mark. I've been playing at the West End, next to the Iowa College where we were.
Um, just the two of you played, then you played the, uh, trumpet, uh, Maurice on that. And, uh, Fess played the, uh, the accordion, huh?

The accordion. The accordion. We used to go all over and play like that, you know. And it sure sounds good. Yeah. Perfect song. Perfect song. Perfect song. Perfect song. Yeah. And we, we used to knock that number out.

And don't forget to tell him about, uh, your friend, uh, who was at his house yesterday, Emmis White. Oh yeah. Oh yeah, he's talking about everybody. And he spoke about Jeff, Greta Jeff, Brian Rice, great musician, and his band.
Yeah, I was in his-
When did you play with him?
I joined the band in, in 19, 1918. Uh, in Kansas City.
Oh, you joined up there?
Yeah. You see, I was in the army.
Oh, that's right.

Yeah. And, uh, we had a 32, I think it was a 32 piece band. We formed a band in, in, uh, Kansas City, Missouri. And we went to Hoboken, New Jersey. We went over in, uh, England. See? We crossed the English Channel and went over in France. It was our Envoy Doon, Le Havre, and Paris, France, you know. Oh yeah. Then, uh, the band broke up, you know, after the war was over.
All of those pictures you showed us the other night.
Yeah. Yeah. That's his band.
Yeah, that's his band. Yeah, that's his band.

Was Amos White the director? Yeah, he was the director. Bandmaster, in other words. Yeah. And, uh, they had nine trumpet players. And he'd taken me off the trumpet and put me on, on clarinet. He'd flat clarinet. And he taught me how to play.
See?
How did you, how did you like clarinet?
Oh, I played it pretty good. It was much easier than trumpet. Yeah.
He likes it better in that way. Yeah. Uh, I suppose when you started, you had a carnet first, and then when did you change to trumpet? Do you remember? Oh, trumpet was not then.
Huh? Trumpet was not that time.

Oh yeah, I had a trumpet in, in France. The issues of trumpet in 1918. I had a busher trumpet. Yeah, that was out of press. Really? Yeah. I don't know when they came out, but I know the government issues trumpets. Because, uh, White had a york trumpet. You can see on that picture his trumpet. Got a york.
Yeah.
He had a york, all right. He had a york, and I had a bushing. And, uh, we didn't have no corn, nothing but york and bush. So my favorite trumpet is a C.G. Cone, see. That's what I always played.
When you started, did you start on a cornet though?
I started on a cornet, yeah. A short cornet. We'd have those bits in them, you know.
Oh yeah, little tiny areas.

Yeah, A shanks, we call them A shanks, B shanks, and C shanks. Yeah, five bits. Yeah, you could play note for note with the piano with the C shanks. And then they got the B flat shank, you know, longer shanks.
Did they use those C shanks much in the bands, that is in dance artists, when you played with piano? Did you, did they really use them?
No, you used the A shank, you know.
I wonder if they ever used that C very much.
No, you could use it, you know, if you played note for note with the piano. Yeah, like a C melody fax.
Yeah, yeah, that's right.
Well, after the trumpet came out, well then I changed the trumpet, see.
Did you notice much difference in the tone or the feel of it when you...

Oh, when I first, it took, it take me about a week to get used to it. See, when I changed to a trumpet, well I had my cornet right on the side of it, and I'd get tired playing the trumpet, and put it down, and pick up the cornet, see. Until I got used to the tone, because the tone was so far away from me, you know. Pitches fall. So I, eventually I got used to it.
Was there much difference in the blowing? Is one easier, harder to blow?
Well, I think the trumpet is much easier than the cornet. To blow, easier to blow. Yeah, it's easier to blow, yeah. And the mouthpiece they're making now is different too, you know.
As far as the tone goes, do you notice much difference in the tone, if one is more mellow or piercing or anything than the other, or louder or anything?
I think the cornet is louder. I think so. Mm-hmm. The trumpet is, you know, it's...
The tone extends often the trumpet. Yeah. And the cornet is taller than you because it's so bunchy.
Yeah. Yeah, sure. It breaks, you know, it breaks, the tone breaks right quick, see.
Mm-hmm. And you, what kind of a horn do you have now? Is yours con yet?
Oh, CG con. I still have my old CG con that I used to play back there in New Orleans, you know. Yeah, I still got it. And I'm gonna keep it till I die. Yeah, I think you should.
Yeah.
Now and then I'll pick it up and play back the knife. Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
We were talking about the brass bands.
Yeah, you said something about Jimmy Noon?

Oh yes, I was going to ask a little bit more about it, then we'll come back to Jimmy Noon. Yeah. The trombones, did they ever alternate like that, do you think, or did they keep playing most of the time?
What, the trombones?
Yeah, when they had two trombones, did they work that same system usually?
No, you see, when they have two trombones, one playing first, one playing second, you see. Yeah. Well, that's the way they operate.
So they didn't usually take one up and one down?
No, no, no. See, because they have first and second trombones. Yeah. It's not like two solo trumpets. Mm-hmm.
Did you usually use three trumpets then, or the ones like the Umbridge?
Yeah, yeah, you see, they have two solo trumpets and a first trumpet.
Yeah.
Well, I used to like to play a first trumpet, you know. It's different. It's the other words that's a second trumpet. Yeah.
A lower alto part. Yeah, yeah.
A lower, higher too. But sometimes they have lead, cue lead on that for you. A solo for the first trumpet player. Yeah.

Yeah. What other instruments did Manuel have in his band that you can remember? What does the whole personnel, like two bands, if you can go down the whole list, remember how they lined up, sort of? You mean the brass band?
The brass band on the street, yeah, like the Onward band.
Yeah. Well, he had the, I, I, I.
The Imperial band, I think. No, Onward.
The one on the street.

Yeah, the Imperial band was the, was the, the last one. Yeah. I couldn't call all the names of them. No, but I mean the, the different instruments, like there was tuba and were there saxophones or what were they? He had a, he had a tuba, one tuba, two trombones, baritone, alto, and a clarinet. Did I say baritone? Yeah.
That was the alto horn and not the alto sax. No, alto horn.

Yeah, like a mellophone or something. And he had two trumpets, just him and I on trumpet. Yeah. And drum, snare drum and bass drum. Yeah. And then later days he put a clarinet in it, had a clarinet in it. Another clarinet?
You mentioned one clarinet, was that? Did I mention a clarinet?
Did you mention clarinet? Yeah. Well, that, that was the band consist of, you know, those men.
Drum and bass, about snare drum and bass drum.
Yeah. Yeah, snare drum and bass drum.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. That fills it out. Yeah. But did they use any saxes in those days, like they do now? They all had saxes on the band.
Well, they, they, they, we had saxes in later days, you know. Later days. Yeah, later days. They had Adolph Alexander playing sax, you know. But not in the old days.
No. They had clarinet.
See, but they, they used saxophone in the, in the later days. And the Imperial band, you know what that band? Yeah.
Did you play in the Imperial band with Manuel, or was that just his dance band? No.
No, that, that was his dance band.
Well you're playing Imperial brass band now.

Yeah, Imperial brass band. Yeah. And the, and the Onward brass. No, it was, it was the, the Onward. Oh, the Imperial, you're right, you're right, it was the Imperial. You know, I forgot about that. You see. Yeah. You know, you met in the Imperial? Yeah.
No, I can't think of it. You remember who was in that first?
You know first? Yeah.

He had, his self-lead, Emmanuel Perez. Yeah. He had, his self-lead, Emmanuel Perez. Yeah. Maurice Duran, Solaris. Right? Maurice Duran, Solaris. Yeah, two, like Maurice said that. Yeah. And I had a first B-flat trumpet player, James McNeil's son. Uh-huh.
Mike Neil, a young boy.
You're right, you're right. Great man.
And, uh, all right.

That's the trumpet section. You're right, you're right. And, alright, that trumpet section. Well, that person, trombone. Earl Humphrey. Earl Humphrey at least, trombone. Yank Johnson trombone. And they had, I played baritone.
You remember that? That's the one when they got through the horn.
Jim Bull played bass horn. What they call Jim Bull.
Don't know anything about him.
Big tall dog fella? Yeah. Jim Bull. All right. At Eddie Sherry. Clarinet.
Did he play E flat? You remember?
No, he played B flat. Respectful B flat. All low pitch. Low pitch. And they had, they had Arthur Alexander, citrophone. And they had, uh, Henry Martin, snare drum.
Alfred Wilson, snare drum.
Alfred William, snare drum. Alfred William, snare drum. Henry Martin, bass drum.
No, no, that's come to me now. Imperial bass drum. Imperial bass drum.
That was the Imperial. That was after Emanuel's, uh, uh, Onward band then. Mm-hmm. Is that right? Yeah. First it had the Onward. Yeah.
I think the Onward.
Oh, wait a while.
I think the Onward. We leave out a man. Pardon me. We leave out a man. Who was that?
Walter Pichon alto.
Oh, yeah. I forgot. You told me.
You told me once he played alto on the one. Yeah, that's right. The piano player.
The Onward. You see, the Onward, the original Onward brass band was, uh, Manny Perez and, uh, Joe Oliver, wasn't it?
I believe so.
Well, I tell ya.

They are, they're organized, an Onward brass band. Manny Perez, leader. Solaris, Andrew Kimball Solaris. Peter Buckeyes, voice trumpet. Buddy Johnson. Trombone. Trombone. Vic Gasper trombone. And, uh, I had, uh, the Rensitio clarinet. And I had, uh, old man, Tatan. Biotan. Adolf Paul. Yeah. Oh, Alexander, huh? Yeah, Adolf Alexander. The old man. He's called Tatan. Tatan, yeah. And I had for Alto, old man Bob Murray. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Paul's father. Yeah. Still living, by the way. He's still there. I couldn't think of it. Well, it has, for baritone, Ed Atkins.
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . For bass drum, Dan DeLewis. And bass horn, tuba horn, Eddie Jackson. And, uh, well, the bass drum at Bebe Matthews. That's the arm was, the arm was they had.
Was Joe Oliver in that sometimes?

No, not that bad, it was the arm was they had. That's during the time. I had, the district had clothes from the tuxedo dance hall, changed it into a villa. I was playing there and Eddie Atkins was playing drum on me. And Joe Howard was playing trumpet.
And Maurice, do you remember Eddie Jackson, anything about him?

Oh yeah, I used to play in the tuxedo brass band with him. Oh yeah, he's a pretty good bass player. He gives you plenty of help. See I played with, I joined the tuxedo brass band when Celestane gave up playing. See I played with Louis DuVean, see. Him and I was leading, he was leading the band, I was playing solo too. Yeah, Eddie Jackson's a wonderful musician.
And then Jackson, he went on bass violin. He played with the Nola band. Yeah. Nola. Pete Lacoste, the trumpet player.
Yeah. Well I taught Pete Lacoste. I taught him trumpet. You taught him trumpet?
Yeah.

Yeah. And you know like the band, the jazz band would meet on Sundays on advertising and buck against one another. Yeah. So I'd pull up there by Pete Lacoste and he'd be trembling, you know. Thought I was going to buck against him. I wouldn't buck. I'd just wave, you know, and go by. And me and Rene never did buck. And then Buddy Petit, we never did buck together, you know. But Punch and all them other trumpet players, you know. Chris Kelly? Yeah. Chris Kelly. They stopped in the back there, that time they had mule wagons, you know, and horse and stuff. They'd back the tailgate to each one together like that and let's play. Sometimes we'd be there three and four hours, one play and the other play, you know. Just on one corner. Yeah, on one corner. We wouldn't have time to finish advertising, you know. So I'll never forget, we was on Gravia and I was somewhere back that we were playing. I was playing with Frankie Dusen then. And we was playing, you know, music like Sally Trombone and all that kind of stuff, you know. And old Jack Carey, they was playing all kinds of different numbers. And we would run them away, we would run them off that corner. See, they left. And when Punch got way down to the next corner line there, I said, watch her calling back. I said, you need to know it, because I don't know how to play no blues like him, you know. I start to play in the blues. Punch said, stop, stop, stop, turn around. Then he turned to the wagon around and come back up there and we pull off and laugh at him.
He wouldn't even stay there and fight it out.

No, no. We was putting some music on them, you know. Sally Trombone, Miss Trombone and all that kind of stuff. And old Frankie Dusen was laying right in it, you know. Willie Humphrey was playing with us then. We had a good band, Lil' Alec playing bass. I done forgot who was playing drum. Pretty good band then.
Do you remember any of the halls you played when you were advertising? In which places were you playing the dances?

Boy, yeah, I played in the Economy Hall. I played in the Santa Sena Club. I played in the Bulls Club. And I played in the Hopes Hall. Sacred Hall of Mary's in the Algea's? Yeah, I played in the Sacred Hall in the Algea's. And it's a hall uptown I used to play on. St. Elizabeth? I played in St. Catherine Hall. I played on the Steamer Capital.
Oh yeah, I forgot to ask you to go over.
Yeah, I played up there when Faith Marble had his band, Durant and Humphrey. We had Durant and Humphrey at the time we played up there. You know, two bands. Hour on, hour off. Oh, two on the boat?
Yeah, they had two bands.

See the boat had their own band, you know, Faith Marble. So Stratford hired me, hired our band, you know, the relief of them, hour on, hour off. And then after that he heard how I played and everything. And he sent Kimber, you know the best player of Faith?
Henry Kimber?
Yeah, he sent him to my house to try to get me to play, join the band, you know. Well, I didn't want to quit my band, you know. Go play on the boat.
When you played on the boat it was just there at New Orleans, you didn't go up the river
to St. Louis or anything like that? No, no, no. It was a single engagement, you know.
Yeah, mm-hmm.
Ever so often they get different bands, you know. Extra boat ride. Yeah, extra boat ride, you know. Yeah. They go further up the river than they usually go, you know.
Yeah, like an all day excursion, things like that sometimes. Yeah, all day excursion, yeah. So we were going to talk about Jimmy Noon a minute ago. If you can remember, tell me about.
Well, I'll tell you, Jimmy Noon, he born on St. Menard Pass where I was born, you know. And he used to play a ghetto.
Well, by the way, before we go on, just what part of it, was it down as far as Violet or?
No, it was Merrillville. Merrillville. Merrillville. Merrillville. That's about three miles full, you get to Chip Allen Canal, which is called Violet. It's past Chalmette then.
Oh yeah, yeah.
It's past Chalmette. And the next little village is the Parish Road. Then the next is Corrine. See, that's where I was born at, Corrine.
Corrine, yeah.

And then the next is Merrillville. See? The next is Walkers, Stories, and then Highland and Ship Island Canal, or the woods, Violet. It was there, Violet. You see? Well, as I was going to say about Jimmy.
Excuse me for interrupting, but I wanted to know just where you were born, too.

Yeah. I was born in Corrine. That's in Seminard Paris. And we used to go down to Merrillville, you know, they had a big store down and all the bars would be on the front gallery, you know. And he'd have the guitar playing it, you know, and we'd be dancing and going on like that. So he stayed there a while and he went and Freddie Kepard was going with his sister, you know, Sister Noon, and he advised him to put the banjo, the guitar down, and learn clarinet. So he did. Old man Chalineese is what I want to call the name that night.
I called Chalineese the other night.

Yeah. Well he was the one that learned Jimmy Noon sax, or clarinet. Clarinet? Yeah. Well then Jimmy Noon played with Freddie Wilde, he played with Manuel, and he played with Joe Oliver. Then he left and he went to Chicago, and he played with Cooks, I think it was Cook.
Yeah, for a long time. St. Cyr was with that band too.
Yeah, he played with Cook. Then after a while he organized a band of his own, Guy Kelly. Used to play with Celestine, I played with him, you know. And the last time I heard about him he died in L.A.
Yeah, he came out here to California in about 1943 or so, along in there. He said when you were little kids or babies practically, you used to all sleep together, was it?

Well, his sister, he know he got three sisters. No, he had two sisters. No, he had three sisters. He had two bright ones. But how about one of those sisters? Yeah. That was Lindsay. Yeah, well you see when they would, when Big I Louie, and we called him Big I Louie, but it's Louie DeLia.
Yeah, I know, I knew him very well.

Yeah. Well he would come down home, my mother and them used to give dances on Saturday night. Down in the country? Yeah, down in the Merrillville down there. Not Merrillville, but Corrine where I was born. And it was Big I Louie, Henry Fould, Mitchell, Albert Mitchell, and Johnny Gould.
Johnny Gould. Yeah.
I played with them.
Yeah.

They used to come down there and play. Well they'd come play on Saturday night and they wouldn't come home, they wouldn't come to New Orleans until Monday morning. See? Well them girls would come right on over and call my mother Annie Marie. And they'd get in the bed right with us, you know. Well we was all young then, you know.
Yeah, sure. See?
And that's how I come to know Jimmy Noon.
Well, since he isn't here anymore, we'll never get all those facts from him. Are his sisters, any of them living? Do you think? Are they all dead?

See? He had two sisters, three sisters.

segments.title: Recording starts
segments.summary: Interviewer gets the recording going and tells Durand to sit anywhere.

segments.title: Durand's birthplace and first lessons from his uncle and Professor Humphrey
segments.summary: Durand gives his name, address and birth in 1893 below New Orleans. His uncle in the Terminal Brass Band gave his first lesson, then he studied with Jim Humphrey.

segments.title: Family, uncles and religion
segments.summary: Neither parent played; two uncles were musicians. Durand has no middle name and is Catholic.

segments.title: Trumpet and the bands he played with, including Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Trumpet was his only instrument. He lists the bands he played in, played accordion duets with Fess Manetta, and worked in Perez's orchestra then the Onward Brass Band.

segments.title: The Durand and Humphrey band and its personnel
segments.summary: Durand led a band with Willie Humphrey, whose grandfather Jim taught Durand. He names the members.

segments.title: Childhood listening: Freddie Keppard, Big Eye Louis and the Terminal band
segments.summary: As a boy he followed Keppard and sat in, and played Shoulder Strap. He recalls the Terminal Brass Band members and following Perez and Oliver.

segments.title: Favorite trumpeter Perez, lessons with Humphrey and the Arban method
segments.summary: Perez was his favorite but sent him to Humphrey. He studied the Arban method and later got ideas from Fess Manetta.

segments.title: Playing parties with Fess Manetta and the bass player Johnny Predonce
segments.summary: Anecdotes of party jobs with Manetta on accordion and Johnny Predonce on bass.

segments.title: Army band in Kansas City and France under Amos White
segments.summary: He joined Amos White's army band in 1918 in Kansas City, went to France, and was switched to clarinet.

segments.title: Cornet versus trumpet, shanks and tone
segments.summary: Government-issue trumpets, cornet shanks, and the differences in tone and blowing between cornet and trumpet.

segments.title: His C.G. Conn horn
segments.summary: He still owns the old Conn he played in New Orleans and will keep it.

segments.title: Trombone and trumpet parts in brass bands
segments.summary: How two trombones and the first and solo trumpets are arranged in a street band.

segments.title: Instrumentation of Perez's Onward and Imperial brass bands
segments.summary: Durand describes the instruments in Perez's street band, saxophones in later days, and the Imperial confusion.

segments.title: Imperial and Onward Brass Band personnel lists
segments.summary: The second interviewer reads the Imperial and Onward lineups while Durand corrects.

segments.title: Eddie Jackson and the Tuxedo Brass Band
segments.summary: Durand recalls playing with bassist Eddie Jackson in the Tuxedo Brass Band, and teaching Pete Lacoste trumpet.

segments.title: Advertising wagon battles with Punch Miller and Jack Carey
segments.summary: Bands bucked wagon to wagon on street corners; Durand with Frankie Dusen ran Punch off the corner.

segments.title: Halls where he played dances
segments.summary: He lists the halls he played in New Orleans.

segments.title: Relief band on the Streckfus steamer
segments.summary: His band alternated hour on, hour off with the boat band; he declined to join and played only local excursions.

segments.title: Where Durand was born and Jimmy Noone's origins
segments.summary: The geography of St. Bernard Parish villages and that Noone was born where Durand was.

segments.title: Jimmy Noone's path from guitar to clarinet and Chicago
segments.summary: Keppard advised Noone to switch to clarinet; Noone played with Perez and Oliver, went to Chicago and died in L.A.

segments.title: Noone's sisters and family, and country dances at Durand's home
segments.summary: Country dances at Durand's mother's house and Noone's sisters, funeral and family.

segments.title: Giving up trumpet, mop factory and the Ninth Ward home
segments.summary: Pay fell to 75 cents a night, so he quit music, made mops, and moved to California in 1944; he recalls the Ninth Ward house.

segments.title: Country bands and who hired them for dances
segments.summary: Country dances hired city musicians; local accordion and banjo bands played plantations. Closing check for other bands.

segments.title: Playing by ear and by memory
segments.summary: He read music but memorized numbers and embellished them, playing loud or soft.

segments.title: Early recording and warming up on the trumpet
segments.summary: He made an early cylinder record playing Turnip Greens, and warms up for a demonstration.

segments.title: High notes and non-pressure playing
segments.summary: Durand explains playing high with little pressure, a trick Willie Humphrey told him of.

segments.title: Mutes
segments.summary: He used wah-wah mutes, kazoos, a plunger and cans.

segments.title: Thanks and close
segments.summary: Interviewer thanks Durand.
